description_block:
JACKIE LEAF ROOKIE!!!... The immortal Jackie Robinson may not be the greatest statistical player ever, but his monumental color barrier-breaking 1947 season is one of America's most earth-shattering and historic events! Hobbyists scramble to collect Jackie's high-end baseball cards, such as the one offered here, his 1948 Leaf #79 rookie card in a fine SGC 6 EX-NM holder. What else can we say about this immortal Hall of Famer that hasn't already been said? What he had to endure as a ballplayer in order to change the game was abuse that no person should have to go through, but he did so reluctantly in anticipation of its ultimate outcome on inclusion for all. But far beyond, Jackie Robinson’s courage and strength of character were his excellent playing abilities. 
 
At the start of his career, Jackie was named the 1947 National League Rookie of the Year and then won the 1949 NL MVP. He led his Dodgers to six pennants and a World Series title in 1955, stole bases, hit for average and power, fielded his position flawlessly, and, like Ty Cobb, was as fiery a competitor as the game had ever seen. The immortal Jackie Robinson's 1948 Leaf rookie card easily stands as his most treasured cardboard artifact. His classic portrait pose turns back the clock to when this courageous legend changed baseball forever, and like most examples, it does reveal a somewhat off-registered image. 
 
Most significantly, the exalted illustration portrays near-perfect centering between four off-white borders, and it's surely no secret that finding an extremely well-centered 1948 Leaf Jackie is an excruciating task. Spotted toning, subtle, though minimal, corner wear consistent with the grade, and the lack of any obtrusive surface flaws complete this cardboard treasure that has rightfully earned its 6 EX-NM evaluation. Incredibly, Robinson's remarkable skill set is overshadowed by his everlasting stature, with Jackie's momentous 1947 Brooklyn Dodgers contract marking an end to the unjust suppression of talented African-American ballplayers for some 75+ years. This #79 Jackie serves as one of the key anchors to the coveted 1948 Leaf release along with #4 Stan Musial, #32 Warren Spahn RC, #138 Larry Doby and #224 Satchel Paige, among many other stars and Hall of Famers.

description_block: In 1923, Christy Mathewson was more than six years removed from the mound, having already posted one of the greatest records of any pitcher in history. Christy Mathewson amassed a 373-188 record with 2,507 strikeouts and posted a sensational 2.13 ERA over 636 games, 435 of which he completed. Following his ultimate retirement from pitching, Mathewson served in the U.S. Army’s Chemical Warfare Service in France during World War I, where he was exposed to mustard gases and eventually contracted tuberculosis, an ailment that would in the end cause his death. Traveling to and from Saranac Lake, New York to the Trudeau Sanitarium, where he was originally diagnosed with TB, Mathewson had hopes of returning to the game, and friend and former manager John McGraw advocated on behalf of the Christian Gentleman. Despite a concerted effort to have Bix Six return to baseball as a manager, Christy’s illness won the battle, and he passed in October of 1925 in Saranac Lake, NY. Presented here is a Christy Mathewson handwritten and signed check to G. A. Toupin & Co., a women’s clothier, in Saranac Lake on “Jan. 4, 1923”. The check has been signed in black fountain pen and PSA/DNA has encapsulated this Authentic, and appears “8-9” strength. Delightful Hall of Famer signed check.

HIGH-GRADE BOWMAN JACKIE!!!... Jackie Robinson breaking the MLB color barrier in 1947 will always stand as our National Pastime's most historical event. For this reason, hobby enthusiasts gravitate towards Jackie's high-end baseball cards, and one of them is offered here, his 1950 Bowman subject in an astonishing SGC 8 NM-MT holder. To date, SGC has encapsulated nearly 900 Jackie Robinson #22 examples, with only seven equaling this high-grade 8 and one graded higher. Jackie Robinson's diamond achievements include a 1947 Rookie of the Year, an MVP award in 1949, leading the Dodgers to six pennants and a World championship in 1955, and he was renowned as one of the fiercest competitors in the game. Yet, for all of his stellar accomplishments, his place in baseball history will forever be correlated with being the first African American to play Major League Baseball, forever changing the National Pastime for the better. 
 
Presented here is a brilliant 1950 Bowman #22 Jackie in an SGC holder, one of the finest we’ve seen, starting with his picturesque batting pose that exhibits near-perfect resolution, vibrant color and wonderful centering. An incredible array of blue, green, brown, and grey hues create a museum quality image framed by four somewhat lightly toned borders. His strength of character as well as his play equally assisted in earning him the coveted trophy. Only two years later, his strength and abilities were on display once more as he captured the 1949 MVP Award, affirming Branch Rickey’s notion that the league would be a better product if truly the best players, no matter their race, were included. From 1947 to 1956, Robinson’s entire career, he led the Brooklyn Dodgers to six National League pennants and a 1955 World Championship. 
 
Presented here is a breathtaking PSA 8 NM-MT 1953 Topps #1 Jackie Robinson that has only been bested by eleven of the more than 4,600 PSA encapsulated examples! Four blinding white borders and the virtually impeccable surfaces serve to accentuate the brilliantly bold central image of Brooklyn’s greatest utility player. This extraordinary pack-fresh masterpiece truly resides as one of his most celebrated and finest preserved cardboard treasures!

description_block: MID-GRADE HONUS!!!... This outstanding PSA 5 EX 1909 E92 Dockman & Sons Honus Wagner Throwing heirloom has rightfully earned its assessment. A bona fide POP 3 offering, it has only been bested by a paltry four examples on the combined PSA and SGC census reports, a testament to its irrefutable paucity level at the highly coveted mid-grade plateau! While there are a reasonable number of high-grade “T” tobacco cards in circulation, the quantity of high-grade “E” caramel subjects is few and far between. This ultimately led to the conundrum of the hobby’s most meticulous collectors floundering in a seemingly endless search for the scant supply of existing “E” cards reflecting 5 EX or better assessments. Historically speaking, the John Dockman & Sons Gum Co. included 50 different baseball card subjects with their brand product issued during the 1909 season. That year Wagner would win his first and only world championship, besting Ty Cobb’s Detroit Tigers in a tightly contested seven-game series. By 1909, Honus Wagner had established himself as our National Pastime’s greatest player.  Going into the 1909 season, Wagner had already compiled six NL batting titles, with his .339 average in 1909 good enough to once again pace the Senior Circuit and lead Pittsburgh to their inaugural World Series title. Hans would win his still NL record eighth batting title two years later, eventually retiring with a stellar .328 mark and the title of “baseball’s greatest all-time shortstop.” Like that distinction, this unprecedented masterpiece has outdistanced most of its inferior peers. The revered Wagner throwing pose reveals a sparkling array of blue, orange, green and yellow hues that bring the Honus illustration to life. You can feel Wagner’s intensity as he completes a throw across the infield, with the classic image favoring the right edge between four somewhat toned borders. No obtrusive surface flaws are evident, and preventing a higher assessment is even corner wear as well as what appears to be some factory-issued diminutive print marks along the upper border. The final exclamation point is the critical "JOHN H. DOCKMAN & SONS” ad back, with most of the superb technical attributes defying the past 115 years. This elusive PSA 5 masterpiece stands tall as one of Wagner’s finest.

description_block:
Prior to even his birth, Mickey Mantle was destined for a life on the baseball diamond. Mutt Mantle, Mickey’s father and former semi pro ballplayer, named his boy after his idol Mickey Cochrane, despite the fact that Cochrane’s given name was Gordon. Mickey later quipped that “I would have hated to be named Gordon.” But The Mick’s path was set as Mutt taught him the game and even taught him the art of pinch-hitting. “Dad would pitch to me right-handed… Grandpa would pitch to me lefty…” Near-daily sandlot games as a boy and then high school ball honed Mickey into a muscular ballplayer with tremendous power. Yankees scout Tom Greenwade, there to look at one of Mick’s teammates, witnessed the 16-year-old Mantle crush two home runs on a scouting visit (one left-handed and one right-handed) and persuaded Mutt & Mick to sign with New York upon his graduation from high school. Struggles did ensue during his rookie year, so Mutt had to once again step in to figuratively “level a double-barreled shotgun at my head” to get the Commerce Comet back on track, but that was the end of any significant slump or doubts. Mutt sadly passed in 1952, but Mickey went on to become one of the greatest ball players the game had ever seen, even better than Mickey Cochrane. 
 
Presented here is by far the most significant Topps baseball card ever produced and the anchor of the artistic 407-card 1952 Topps set, #311 Mickey Mantle which has been holdered 5 EX by PSA.  This is one of the most striking examples of the flawless artistry represented in the 1952 Topps series as the color and cleanliness pull you in to take a good long look. It’s not too often that an image from this most coveted of Mantle issues stands out so prominently, no matter the grade. At first glance, the image is skewed only mildly to the right, and the borders are strong and white. Looking slightly closer, light flaking along the border, mild soiling and a minimally nicked upper right edge are evident. Evenly worn corners and some inconsequential adhesive residue can be seen on the back. However, the central subject of the boyish Commerce Comet remains untouched and/or unblemished as he gazed up awaiting his turn at bat. 
 
The Mick would surpass his namesake, Mickey Cochrane, winning three American League MVPs to Cochrane’s two, but his power earned him 536 home runs against Cochrane’s 119. He also won seven World Series titles to Cochrane’s three. While Mutt’s expectations were certainly high, Mickey Mantle became everything that his father thought he might be and more. To millions of fans, Mickey Mantle was an American hero!

description_block:
CONTROL! CONTROL! CONTROL!!!... “You’ve got to have control. Without control, you’re nothing!” Sage advice that Ed Spahn gave to his lanky left-handed son, Warren. A former semipro ballplayer himself, Ed taught Warren how to throw without strain and use the high leg kick as a form of deception, which batters later conveyed it was like the ball came out of his uniform. Despite wanting to be the next Lou Gehrig, Warren didn’t have the frame as a wiry, skinny kid, so he was groomed to be a pitcher. In high school, he made the switch for good. As a minor leaguer, Spahn moved quickly through the ranks, going 41-22 in 63 games before Boston called him up. In ’41, he threw 42 consecutive scoreless innings and three one-hitters. Exceptional! But his country soon came calling, and after only four appearances in 1942, Spahn spent three years in the Army and returned to join the big-league roster in 1946. 
 
From 1946 to 1964, in Boston and then Milwaukee, Warren Spahn had only two losing seasons (1952 & 1964). Using the fundamentals that his father ingrained in him, Warren Spahn was one of the most resilient workhorses in baseball, averaging 32 starts during the span of 1946-64. He posted a record of 356-229, struck out 2,486 batters and had a 3.04 ERA over those 18 seasons. He led the NL in wins eight times and cleared the 20-win mark 13 times. In 1957, he led the Braves to the World Series titles and captured the NL Cy Young as he went 21-11. However, one of the most remarkable feats of the lanky lefty was that over his 21 years in the big leagues, he hit only 42 batters of the more than 21,500 batters faced and never more than six in a season. And ... he only threw 81 wild pitches. Just amazing. Warren Spahn retired after 21 seasons with a record of 363-245, a 3.09 ERA and 2,583 Ks in 750 games. In 665 starts, Spahn had 382 complete games and 63 shutouts. 
 
Offered is a 1948 Leaf #32 Warren Spahn graded 9 MINT by PSA. High-grade examples seldom emerge for auction, and the offered issue presents every attribute expected from a PSA 9 with a crystal-clear portrait of Spahn set against a striking pumpkin orange backdrop with sensational centering, super clean borders, extremely sharp corner tips and immaculate surfaces. This is without equal as the finest Warren Spahn Rookie Memory Lane has ever had the pleasure to offer. With only three equals and only a single GEM MINT 10 ever holder, this breathtakingly bright and colorful Spahn is sure to upgrade even the finest Registry Set.

description_block:
Only 10 or 15 years ago, the talk of the hobby was often centered around the so-called “Holy Grail” of sports cards, the iconic and incredibly rare 1909-11 T206 White Border Honus Wagner which was fetching unbelievable money, $1.27M in 2000. However, Mickey Mantle’s 1952 Topps #311 has closed the gap and even surpassed the “Wagner” as the most expensive baseball card in existence with an SGC 9.5 topping the $12.6-million mark in 2022. It would seem that given that the Wagner, last sold in 2007 for the sum of $2.8M, may forever be off the market considering that its last sale was nearly 20 years past. But that is not the case for The Mick. Memory Lane has the distinct honor to offer three 1952 Topps #311 Mickey Mantle in this auction alone. 
 
Starting in 1951, Mickey Mantle joined the New York Yankees with high expectations as the successor to the beloved Yankee Clipper, Joe DiMaggio. The Commerce Comet ably took the reins of the Yankees offense, and though he didn't reach the nine World Series wins that DiMaggio achieved, he led the Bronx Bombers to seven titles over his 18-year career. In 1956, he became the 10th player since 1900 to capture the elusive Triple Crown after leading the American League in batting (.353), home runs (52) and RBIs (130) to win his first of three AL MVP awards, tying Joltin’ Joe with a trio. Despite injuries plaguing the Oklahoma Kid throughout his career, including a torn ACL suffered in a collision with Joe D in 1951, Mickey Mantle became one of the most beloved and most dominant ballplayers to ever don the pinstripes. His 18 World Series home runs still stand as a record even 61 years after his last playoff appearance. He is an American hero to a generation of fans. 
 
As previously mentioned, Memory Lane has the distinct honor to offer three 1952 Topps #311 Mickey Mantle “Rookies” including this example holdered 5.5 EX+ by SGC. Displaying a fantastic lithographic image of The Mick looking over his shoulder, bat in hand, against a blue-green background, this issue is sharp. Showing obvious favoritism toward the left edge, the borders remain white and clean with only the slightest of touches on the corners. The surfaces, however, appear pristine with no evident defects and a reverse that is as sharp as the day it was printed. Though there will forever be an air of mystique around the Wagner and the value astronomical, Mickey Mantle’s Rookie will continue to boast its place as the most expensive and highly sought-after post-WWII issue in the hobby

MONTANA ROOKIE!!!... Much like Pittsburgh's Bradshaw in the 1970s, Joe Montana led the San Francisco 49ers to four Super Bowl titles (SBs: XVI, XIX, XXIII & XXIV). Joe Cool is widely considered the best quarterback from the 1980s, especially high praise considering his tenure overlapped with Miami’s Marino, Denver’s Elway, San Diego’s Fouts and New York’s Simms. But it all started in South Bend, Indiana when he led the Notre Dame Fighting Irish to the 1977 National Championship. Recruited by Ara Parseghian, Montana made the varsity squad as a sophomore under Dan Devine, leading the latter to his only national title during his tenure at ND. Leading the 10-1 Fighting Irish, Montana led the underdog Notre Dame to an unlikely 38-10 upset of the undefeated Texas Longhorns with fellow Hall of Famer Earl Campbell coming out of the backfield. Drafted in the third round of the 1979 NFL Draft, Joe was soon to replace Steve DeBerg as the #1 starting QB in only his third season as he led the Niners to the first Super Bowl of his tenure. 
 
Having successfully turned the San Francisco 49ers franchise around, from 1980 to 1989, Joe Montana amassed 30,958 passing yards and 215 touchdowns, many of which were caught by Hall of Famer Jerry Rice. He is often referred to as the Comeback Kid due to his career 28 game-winning drives and 26 4th quarter comebacks. One such comeback came in this first championship season as he rifled a pass to wide receiver Dwight Clark in the NFC Championship game against the Cowboys to complete a game-winning drive, leaving only 51 seconds on the clock. “The Catch”, captured on film from behind the end zone, is one of the most recognizable and frequently played replays during the playoffs each year. 
 
Presented here is a 1981 Topps #216 Joe Montana Rookie issue holdered PSA GEM MINT 10. This is one of the hobby's most iconic cards; this Joe Montana Rookie is spectacular; hence it landed inside a PSA 10 GEM MINT holder. Perfectly centered with four razor-sharp borders terminating at pinpoint corner tips, the image of Joe Cool remains clear as day with the back as impeccable as the front. Ready to complete one of his perfect passes, this rookie of the Comeback Kid should be on every gridiron collector’s radar and is destined for the finest of rookie NFL collections!

Growing up on “The Hill”, the famed Italian neighborhood in St. Louis, Larry and neighbor, Joe Garagiola, played baseball at every turn. When the boys were around 15 years old they were offered a tryout with the hometown Cardinals and Garagiola accepted a contract and $500 bonus. Berra was not offered the bonus, so he held out and eventually the Yankees got word of his abilities, giving him a $500 bonus and $90 monthly salary as he signed on the dotted line in 1943. Berra spend two years in the service WWII, but returned to the Yankees lineup as a utility player until finally taking up permanent residence behind home plate for New York for the next near-two decades. 
 
Undoubtedly rostered with New York during the club’s heyday, Yogi won the World Series in his first season and, in fact, in the first six years that his club went to the postseason. But Berra wasn’t riding the coattails of the likes of Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, Phil Rizzuto or Whitey Ford, he was a catalyst in the Yankees lineup that won games defensively behind the plate and at bat. Yogi Berra never solely led a single offensive category during his 19 MLB seasons, but he was honored with three American League MVPs and 18 All-Star nods. Absolutely remarkable for a small kid from the Gateway City. Berra’s three AL MVP awards came when the likes of Ted Williams, Al Kaline and Mickey Mantle were on top of their games. Ultimately, over the course of his 19 years in the big leagues, he batted .285 with 358 home runs and 1,430 RBIs. Yogi was one of the most respected catchers in Major League Baseball history.

This one of only a couple handfuls has been bested by only a single GEM MINT 10 example which we had the pleasure of selling in 2017. This remains one of the most sought-after rookies in existence, so DO NOT let this Yogi Berra 1st-year card slip through your fingers.

Presented here is an extremely scarce for the grade 1909 T206 Ty Cobb “Bat On Shoulder” Sweet Caporal 350 Subjects/Factory 25 marvel that just happens to be one of only two examples at this highest graded level for this particular ad back. Indeed, this low-pop PSA 8 NM-MT Cobb “Bat On Shoulder” subject is arguably one of the most desirable turn-of-the-century baseball cards of the four different Ty Cobb T206 cards issued between 1909 and 1911 by the American Tobacco Company (ATC). The Georgia Peach arguably resides as the supreme baseball legend from that era, and no baseball card carries his legacy more prominently than a high-grade T206 artifact. 
 
Going into the 1909 campaign, Tyrus had already claimed two consecutive American League batting championships, and his .377 mark in 1909 also paced the Junior Circuit with a league-leading 216 hits. His record .366 career average, 4,189 safeties, and 12 batting titles over a 13-season stretch (including nine in a row from 1907 to 1915) are the ultimate highlights of his remarkable career. A 1936 HOF Charter Member, any century-old Cobb relic is worthy of Cooperstown cardboard status, let alone an example residing in this awe-inspiring state. Unquestionably, the T206 tobacco issue is the most prestigious group of pre-WWI cards and enthusiasts scramble to obtain at least one, if not all four, of the Ty Cobb T206 variations in high-grade, with all four Cobb's included in PSA's illustrious Top 250 Sportscards in the hobby publication. 
 
The offered 1909-11 T206 Ty Cobb “Bat on Shoulder” portrays virtually all of the required attributes associated with a pack-fresh card, starting with the spectacular gray hues on his classic Tigers uniform as well as the detailed intensity emanating from his facial expression. Most impressive is the radiant yellow background, enhanced by a rich array of orange, blue and green hues, portraying an awe-inspiring backdrop. Near-perfect centering, four blinding white borders, right-angled corners, virtually immaculate surfaces, and an extremely bold red Sweet Caporal 350 Subjects back all serve to accentuate the beauty of this coveted Cobb keepsake.

description_block: Issued just after Grover Cleveland Alexander returned from World War I in April 1919, this historic check represents a remarkable moment in baseball history. Dated April 30, 1919, the check was paid to Cubs manager Fred Mitchell and subsequently endorsed to Alexander, who then signed it over to Henry M. Ahern, a Cubs employee. Just weeks later, on May 9, 1919, Alexander would make his first postwar pitching appearance. Alexander’s signature on the reverse is outstanding, and the timing of the transaction adds exceptional historical significance. The front of the check bears the signature of William Veeck Sr., the newly appointed Cubs president. During Veeck’s tenure from 1919 to 1933, the Cubs captured the 1929 and 1932 pennants, and he oversaw the transformation of Wrigley Field into its iconic modern form, complete with ivy-covered walls and concrete outfield bleachers. A rare and meaningful artifact, this check connects three major figures and a pivotal moment in baseball history.

Pack-fresh surfaces and sharp corners complete this 1957 Topps #407, the last card in the set, as more than worthy of a final resting place in any high-grade PSA Registered Set! card_name: 2009 Upper Deck SP Legendary Mystery Cuts Marilyn Monroe Signed Check
special_note: Marilyn Monroe autographs rarely surface, especially in such stupendous condition.
description_block:
The story of Marilyn Monroe is one of sadness, exhilaration, unimaginable fame and ultimately tragedy. Born Norma Jean Mortenson, though it was later determined that Norma’s father was likely Charles Gifford, an executive at RKO Studios. Gladys, Norma’s mother, placed her in foster care as a young girl and she moved from family to family, reportedly suffering sexual abuse on occasion. When she was 16, because her then guardian relocated to West Virginia, Norma was married off to James Dougherty, a young merchant seaman, in order for her to not return to the foster system or an orphanage. But shortly after he shipped out, Norma found work as a model and pinup girl, against his wishes. In 1946, she appeared on 33 magazine covers, caught the eye of Hollywood and divorced Dougherty. 
 
As she learned the craft of acting, Norma took the name Marilyn Monroe as a stage name, dyed her hair platinum blonde and never looked back. Using her sexuality and allure, she landed various roles in the late 1940s and in 1950 she appeared in the critically acclaimed films  All About Eve  and  The Asphalt Jungle , elevating her to ultimately take on much more lucrative roles both in money and in fame. In 1953 Marilyn starred in  Niagara ,  Gentlemen Prefer Blondes  and  How to Marry a Millionaire . In 1954, she founded Marilyn Monroe Productions in order to take control of her own career. And from 1955 to 1959, her films  The Seven Year Itch  (1955) and  Some Like It Hot  (1959) were two box office sensations. She was now Hollywood’s “IT” girl and the most notable woman on the planet. High-profile marriages to retired New York Yankee Joe DiMaggio and playwright Arthur Miller, both ending in divorce, only served to intensify her worldwide fame. Sadly, in 1962, seemingly on top of the world, Marilyn’s life was cut short due to an overdose of barbiturates in her Hollywood home. 
 
The story of Marilyn Monroe continues to mystify and intrigue historians and conspiracy theorists alike, but her fame has virtually never faded. One might be hard pressed to find anyone of teenage or older who hasn’t heard the name Marilyn Monroe. For that reason, we think that this incredible 2010 Upper Deck SP Legendary Cuts Mystery Cuts #LC-MC card featuring a signed Marilyn Monroe check cut, presumably to the Beverly Hills Hotel, a frequent residence of hers, should catch the attention of multiple rare autograph enthusiasts. Handwritten and signed in blue ballpoint, this 2-of-2 is one of the rarities. Marilyn Monroe autographs rarely surface, especially in such stupendous condition as this. If you are a Marilyn Monroe fan or even just a rare signature enthusiast, this phenomenal cut will surely stand as a marquee item of any collection!

If that wasn't enough, before he graced the hardwood court in Boston, he added an Olympic gold medal to his blossoming list of superlatives, leading the 1956 U.S. basketball team to an 89-55 clinching win over the Soviet Union in Melbourne, Australia. 
 
While choosing the finest NBA all-time player is a seemingly impossible task, there are many historians who give Bill Russell this distinguished nod based on his unmatched championship legacy. He claimed five League MVPs and played in 12 All-Star games, with immortal coach John Wooden always claiming that Russell was basketball's greatest all-time defensive player. Save for Montreal Canadiens’ Henri Richard (who also claimed 11 NHL championships), no North American athlete has ever enjoyed Bill Russell's uncanny level of winning the final game of virtually each and every season; not Ruth, Berra, DiMaggio, Gretzky, Jordan, or even Tom Brady. Russell's knack for winning the biggest games has created an unequivocal stature for this iconic basketball center, and it comes as no coincidence that his exalted inaugural Topps card is one of the most sought-after cardboard keepsakes on the planet. 
 
With regard to this cardboard masterpiece's stellar eye appeal, the classic Russell pose boasting his iconic white #6 Celtic jersey retains the majority of its original surface attributes, including fine clarity and a host of sparkling hues. description_block:
POP 1 TICKET!!!... Presented is the ticket stub from the historic rematch game between DeMatha Catholic vs. Power Memorial graded PSA 8 NM-MT with the program and clippings from the original owner who attended the January 30, 1965 game. Rostering the best player in high school at the time, Lew Alcindor, Power Memorial defeated DeMatha Catholic at Univ. of Maryland’s Cole Field House 65-62 in 1964. After three straight Washington, D.C. Catholic League titles, DeMatha Catholic coach Morgan Wootten sought a bigger challenge, and New York’s Power Memorial Academy, with Lew Alcindor, fit the bill as the best in the nation, riding a 46-game win streak. “To be the best, you have to beat the best,” Wootten stated. Aptly named Power Memorial was certainly the best team in organized sports, amateur or professional. With high school’s best player at the time, Lew Alcindor, Power Memorial defeated DeMatha Catholic at Univ. of Maryland’s Cole Field House 65-62 in 1964. The lead-up to the rematch, which took place a year later, was met with as much anticipation as any NBA Game 7 Final and was covered by the prominent newspapers and other sports outlets. In fact, there’s more video footage from this game than even the 100-point game from Wilt Chamberlain in Hershey, PA in 1962. 
 
Coach Wootten and his Stags upended the 71-0 Power Memorial squad in the rematch of January 30, 1965, again at the Cole Field House, to extend their own winning streak to 24-straight. The final score was 46-43 in what is widely considered the greatest game in high school history. Coach Wootten’s unique defensive prowess was to put constant pressure on Alcindor with Bob Whitmore and his teammates. which proved to be the difference, holding him to only 16 points. Coach Wootten is the first high school only basketball coach inducted in the Basketball Hall of Fame. After the game, so impressed and sportsmanlike was Alcindor that he led his team to the DeMatha locker room to offer congratulations. Offered here is the ONE and ONLY graded Student General Admission ticket stub from that monumental game holdered 8 NM-MT by PSA. In superb condition, this is one of the most historic ticket stubs in existence.

WEISER WONDER!!!... Prior to his arrival in Washington, Walter Johnson honed his pitching skills on his family farm in Kansas and in the oil fields in Southern California. Blessed with one of the most dominating arms in MLB history, Johnson described the first time holding a ball as "it settled in the palm of my right hand as though it belonged there and, when I threw it, ball, hand and wrist, and arm and shoulder and back seemed to all work together". Johnson went to pitch for Weiser in the Idaho State League, going 7-1 in 1906 and then 14-2 in 1907 with 214 strikeouts in 146 innings, leading to a miniscule 0.55 ERA. The “Weiser Wonder” was born, though it was short-lived as word got out and the Washington Senators soon came calling. When the Sens signed the big right-hander, he demanded a return train ticket in case things did not work out. They did work out. Johnson ultimately became the second-winningest pitcher in Major League history, posted 11 sub-2.00 ERA seasons (2.17 career), set a still-standing record with 110 strikeouts and completed an astonishing 531 of 666 starts. When the Big Train left Weiser, this captivating Weiser Wonder postcard was produced featuring the young Walter Johnson, glove on his left hand, standing for his team player portrait. 
 
This wonderful correspondence was purchased in the 1910s and then postmarked on August 3, 1918, in Council Bluffs, Iowa. According to the letter, this eastward traveler had a dilemma. Already likely to have travelled for two days leaving Wyoming for Council Bluffs, adding a jaunt to Madison en route to Chicago and then heading back east was out of the question—even for family. That approximate 150 miles would surely have added an additional day or two to the journey of our deliberate traveler, William. But Karl kept this postcard of the great right-hander, and it has survived more than a century of storage and has been encased 1 POOR by SGC. This is the only example of this nature to have been graded by SGC and, to the best of our knowledge, the ONLY one in existence. Posted and stamped, this postcard displays evenly rounded corners and a light watermark at the upper left, possibly having occurred when it was mailed. Some expected surface wrinkles are evident, and the slightest paper loss can be seen on the left border. However, make no mistake that this incredibly rare image is that of Washington’s Big Train, Walter Johnson, at the start of his illustrious Hall of Fame career. *Because there is no specific or definitive date (year) that the Weiser Wonder postcards were produced, our title has been adjusted to encompass the “c. 1910s” decade to reflect the card's SGC label.

description_block:
In 1951, another New York Yankee earned the coveted American League Rookie of the Year Award, but that rookie was not Mickey Mantle. It was Gil McDougald. Only McDougald and Cleveland Indians & Chicago White Sox left fielder Minnie Minoso earned votes, though Mickey posted considerable numbers despite playing only 96 games. A near-career-ending mid season slump that earned him a trip back to the minors to "sort things out" got the Mick back in the game and on track to hit 13 homers and drive in 65 while batting .267 for the year. Mickey would get his, however, as he overcame the pressure of being the next Joe DiMaggio, swatting 536 home runs, earning 20 All-Star invitations, and capturing three American League MVPs and seven World Series titles in 18 seasons. In 1956, Mantle led the league in batting (.353), home runs (52) and RBIs to win the Triple Crown, the MVP and his fourth World Series. More than 50 years after his retirement, Mickey Mantle remains the career home run leader for World Series play with 18 total. The Mick was a genuine role model and, dare I say, superhero to millions of children across the US. 
 
Mickey Mantle's 1952 Topps #311 rookie card IS one of the most sought-after cardboard keepsakes in the hobby. No matter the grade, the 1952 Topps #311 Mickey Mantle is the marquee issue of any baseball card collection or assembly. Considering the desirability of such a cardboard gem, auction companies also hold the 1952 Topps Mantle in the highest regard, prominently featuring the colorful Comet among the highlights and most alluring of offerings. The SGC 9.5 yielding an astonishing $12.6 million in 2022 far surpasses the reasonable budget that Mantle worshippers allot to own a 1952 Topps #311 example of their own. However, according to Vintage Card Prices, PSA 7.5s and down range from under a million dollars, and lower-grade issues have been gotten for under $100,000. So, while the market remains somewhat volatile, ebbing and flowing with continued mind-boggling numbers, it still all comes down to two bidders wanting the same card. 
 
The offered 1952 Topps #311 Mickey Mantle in a PSA 2 GOOD holder is an example that is affordable and desirable for its genuine rarity, color and beauty. This 2 GOOD issue displays even corner wear and strong borders, with brilliant bold colors of the 20-year-old superstar with his bat on his shoulder. With astonishingly clear imagery, this Mick Rookie is as stunning and attractive as multiple contemporaries graded higher at first glance despite the inconspicuous surface wrinkle across the center, beneath his cap. The back is very clean aside from the off-centering favoring the right edge. NOTHING, however, can take away from the beauty of this masterfully designed card featuring one of the greatest players in Yankees and Major League Baseball history.

description_block: THE CHAIRMAN!!!... Arguably the greatest pitcher to ever don the pinstripes, Ford was the ace of six different World Series champion Yankee teams. He completed one of the best seasons ever by a pitcher in 1961, taking home both the Cy Young and World Series MVP awards! Fittingly, he was dubbed the "Chairman of the Board" by teammate Elston Howard for his performances in high-pressure situations. High leverage or not, Ford was consistently dominant throughout his career—his .690 career winning percentage is fourth-best in MLB history. Even more impressive, his 2.75 career ERA is the third lowest among starting pitchers whose careers began post-1920 in the live-ball era. His worst ERA in a single season was 3.24, a tremendous number for essentially everyone else! This is the debut Topps issue for Ford as well as his second-year card due to his service in the Korean War from 1951-1952. This stunner exhibits near-perfect centering, crisp borders, and incredibly detailed imagery. Only eight copies have ever achieved PSA 9 MINT status, making this a truly elite addition to any 1953 Topps collection and one of the best Whitey Ford cards in existence!

description_block: 1 PER HOMER!!!... In the early 1990s, likely ’92, Mickey Mantle’s Restaurant on Central Park South offered a commemorative 18K gold watch with The Mick’s likeness on it for 536 lucky lottery winners, one for each home run he hit during his career. The Swiss quartz watches were numbered 1 to 536 (one for each home run), but it is unknown how many were actually produced of the anticipated 536-watch run. Offered here is a very rare Mickey Mantle 18K gold limited edition watch (#53) featuring the Mick’s likeness on the face with a calfskin leather strap and presented in the original teak box. Based on the number system of one-for-each, Mickey Mantle hit a solo home run to deep right off Virgil Trucks for the 53rd home run of his career on September 1, 1953, in the top of the 7th with the Yankees leading the Chicago White Sox 2-1. He was only 21 but was one of the great hitters of the American League. The Mick would go on to hit 10 times that amount, finishing his career with an astonishing 536 round-trippers. That season he led his New York Yankees to his third World Series title in three years, and he notched two of his World Series record 18 home runs. A certain treasure for any Mickey Mantle enthusiast!

description_block: If you were a baseball fan in the 1920s & ‘30s then the ultimate autograph of the day would have been none other than The Bambino, Babe Ruth himself. And The Babe was more than happy to oblige on most occasions. Living his life as a “big kid” himself, Babe Ruth seemed to adore his fans and droves of youngsters seeking his autograph on anything that they had within arm’s reach. The single-signed Babe Ruth baseball is virtually commonplace as one typically emerges during nearly every auction cycle with Babe Ruth artistically penned on the sphere’s sweet spot in fountain pen. Anything with Ruth’s signature has become a collectible in the hobby including documents, contracts, checks and even automobile registrations. Offered here is a 2012 Historic Autographs The Champions East Coast Edition Baseball Boston 1918 Babe Ruth Cut Signature card graded 8 NM-MT from PSA/DNA. In 1918, only a year before he became a household name as a member of the New York Yankees, Ruth led the Boston Red Sox to their third World Series title in four years and fifth overall. Signed “George H. Ruth” in black fountain pen, this cut was obviously removed from a legal document or contract and affixed to this collectible keepsake. This fantastic signature piece is surely the rarest of the 20-card bunch. Included with the card lot is the original box within which it was presented and purchased.

description_block: With the Red Sox leading the 1912 World Series 1-0-1 against the New York Giants, John McGraw sent starter Rube Marquard to the mound to face the pitching powerhouse of Boston. Boston pitching held American League batters to the second fewest hits and the least number of runs scored in the AL to post a league-best 105-47 record. New York, on the other hand, led the National League in hits, runs, home runs and RBIs for a 103-48 mark. Boston took Game 1 in a 4-3 battle and Game 2 was called due to darkness in the 11th with the teams tied 6-6. Presented here is a Game 3 program from October 10, 1912 that has been meticulously scored and dated in pencil. Our scorer even included pencil notation as to substitutions and replacements as New York eked out a 2-1 victory behind Marquard, who gave up seven hits & one run while striking out six. The program remains in super condition with only minimal storage wear and soiling evident on the front and back covers. The binding is still intact and the program still presents in overall excellent condition!

special_note: Babe Ruth's autograph from a significant historical event
description_block: The 1939-1940 New York World’s Fair was attended by more the 45 million visitors over a near-two-year period, including one George Herman “Babe” Ruth. By 1939, Ruth was well into retirement, spending more time on the golf course and with his wife Claire, than knocking around baseball diamonds. On July 4th, 1939, The Babe was present at Yankee Stadium for Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day, but by this time, his presence was as an ambassador for the game and a draw for the box office. Ruth’s popularity had not diminished in retirement, and when it came time for the World’s Fair, centered in Flushing Meadows, Queens, New York, the Bambino was called upon to assist in promoting the monumental event. The Academy of Sport, the brainchild of Christy Walsh, was established during the World’s Fair, giving kids the opportunity to learn baseball and/or football. Presented here is a sensational program page featuring the Fair’s central focal point, the Trylon, with “Babe Ruth” penned in blue fountain pen within the Perisphere. This exceptional autograph page was evidently removed from a program from the two-season event that spanned 1939 & 1940. This 4-1/2” x 5-1/2” page is in exceptionally high-grade condition and the autograph could easily garner top marks from authenticators. PSA/DNA & JSA LOAs.
